pl-l3d7c1-d1e117.summary: Explains the first opinion's reading: 'God was made man' and 'man was made God' because God began to be a rational substance that had not been, and that substance began to be God, by grace, not by nature or merit. So Christ as man is rightly said to be predestined Son of God.
claims: God began to be a rational substance, which began to be God by grace.
Christ as man is predestined Son of God.

pl-l3d7c1-d1e120.summary: States an objection to the first opinion: if that substance began to be God and God that substance, then some substance is God that was not always God, some substance is God that is not divine substance, and God is something that he always was not.
claims: Objection: the first opinion implies a substance that is God but was not always God.

pl-l3d7c1-d1e123.summary: Reports that they accept this, relying on Origen: he was made what he was not before, but according to the flesh; according to God he was before and there was no time when he was not.
claims: The first opinion accepts that he was made what he was not, according to the flesh.

pl-l3d7c1-d1e130.summary: Notes that the first opinion can be opposed in many other ways, which Lombard omits, leaving the exercise to the reader and hurrying on.

pl-l3d7c1-d1e133.summary: Explains the second opinion's reading: 'God was made man' means he began to subsist from two natures or three substances, and conversely 'man was made God' because the one subsisting in two natures began to be God; or rather because God assumed man and man was assumed by God.
claims: On the second opinion, God began to subsist from two natures.

pl-l3d7c1-d1e136.summary: Cites Augustine, De Trinitate: the assumption was such as to make man God and God man.
claims: The assumption made God man and man God.

pl-l3d7c1-d1e148.summary: Notes that on the second opinion 'God is man' and 'man is God' vary in sense: God is said to be a person subsisting in and from two natures, and the person subsisting from two natures is said to be God, i.e., the Word or the divine nature; the simple person or the nature can be predicated of the composite person. But, as Damascene says, nature and person are not the same.
claims: On the second opinion, 'man is God' predicates the Word or the divine nature of the composite person.

pl-l3d7c1.summary: Explains how each opinion understands the statements. On the first, 'God was made man' and 'man was made God' mean God began to be a rational substance that had not been, and it began to be God by grace, not nature or merit, so Christ as man is predestined Son of God. The objection that some substance is God which was not always God, and is not divine substance, they accept, citing Origen. Lombard declines to pursue further objections. On the second opinion, 'God was made man' means God began to subsist in two natures or three substances, and man was made God because God assumed man. 'God is man' and 'man is God' predicate the composite person or the divine nature of the person; nature and person differ (Damascene).
claims: On the first opinion, God began to be a rational substance, which began to be God by grace.
The first opinion accepts that a substance which was not always God is God.
On the second opinion, God began to subsist in two natures.
On the second opinion, 'God is man' predicates the person or the divine nature.
